question: What do the Colorado Limited Cooperative Association Act, the Wyoming DUNA and DAO LLC statutes, Wyoming's cooperative statute and the Lido, Ooki and bZx decisions establish about which entity a cooperative, non-custodial pool can use, who is a member, how profits and votes are allocated, and who bears liability, as of 2026-10-08?

frame.population: a US cooperative that pools member yield and issues member credit through smart contracts
frame.exposure: C.R.S. 7-58; W.S. 17-32; W.S. 17-31; W.S. 17-10; N.D. Cal. and S.D. Cal. DAO partnership rulings
frame.comparator: unwrapped tokenholder DAO and a conventional cooperative
outcomes: smart-contract immutability under the entity statute

item.title: C.R.S. 7-58-102, Colorado Uniform Limited Cooperative Association Act, definitions

findings.finding: A patron member made a contribution and is required or permitted by the articles or bylaws to conduct patronage with the association to receive or retain the interest.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: “Patron member” means a member that has made a contribution to a limited cooperative association and that: (a) Is required by the articles or bylaws to conduct patronage with the association in the member’s capacity as a patron member in order to receive or retain the member’s interest; or (b) Is permitted by the articles or bylaws to conduct patronage with the association in the member’s capacity as a patron member in order to receive or retain the member’s interest.

findings.finding: An investor member made a contribution and is not required or not permitted to conduct patronage in that capacity.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: “Investor member” means a member that has made a contribution to a limited cooperative association and that: (a) Is not required by the articles or bylaws to conduct patronage with the association in the member’s capacity as an investor member in order to receive or retain the member’s interest; or (b) Is not permitted by the articles or bylaws to conduct patronage with the association in the member’s capacity as an investor member in order to receive or retain the member’s interest.

findings.finding: Patronage is business transactions that entitle a person to financial rights based on the value or quantity of business.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: “Patronage” means business transactions between a limited cooperative association and a person that entitle the person to receive financial rights based on the value or quantity of business done between the association and the person.

item.title: C.R.S. 7-58-104 and 7-58-105, nature and purpose of a limited cooperative association

findings.finding: An LCA is an autonomous, unincorporated association of persons united to meet mutual interests through a jointly owned enterprise, combining patron-member ownership and benefits with separate investments by investor members who may receive returns and a share of control.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: A limited cooperative association organized under this article is an autonomous, unincorporated association of persons united to meet their mutual interests through a jointly owned enterprise primarily controlled by those persons, the patronage of which is carried on for the mutual benefit of the patron members and that permits combining: (a) Ownership, financing, and receipt of benefits by the patron members for whose patronage the association is formed; and (b) Separate investments in the association by investor members who invest in the limited cooperative association and may receive returns on their investments and a share of control.

findings.finding: Relations between an LCA and its members are consensual and contractual; articles and bylaws may provide for any matter not limited by the article or other applicable law.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: The relations between a limited cooperative association and its members are consensual and contractual. Unless required, limited, or prohibited by this article or other applicable law, the articles and bylaws of an association may provide for any matter concerning the relations among the members of the association and between the members and the association, the activities of the association, and the conduct of its activities.

findings.finding: An LCA may be organized for any lawful purpose, whether or not for profit.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: A limited cooperative association may be organized for any lawful purpose, whether or not for profit.

item.title: C.R.S. 7-58-501 and 7-58-511 to 7-58-513, membership minimum and voting

findings.finding: To begin business an LCA needs at least two patron members unless the sole member is a cooperative.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: To begin business, a limited cooperative association must have at least two patron members unless the sole member is a cooperative.

findings.finding: Each patron member has one vote except as the articles or bylaws allocate under 512(1).
findings.exactSourceLanguage: Except as provided by section 7-58-512 (1), each patron member has one vote.

findings.finding: Voting power among patron members may be allocated by one member one vote, use or patronage, equity, or the number of a cooperative member's own patron members, alone or combined.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: The articles or bylaws may allocate voting power among patron members on the basis of one or a combination of the following: (a) One member, one vote; (b) Use or patronage; (c) Equity; or (d) If a patron member is a cooperative, the number of its patron members.

findings.finding: A member denied a use-based vote because it did not use the association in the period must still be allocated at least the minimum voting power of members who did.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: If the articles or bylaws allocate voting power on the basis of use or patronage and a member would be denied a vote because the member did not use the limited cooperative association or conduct patronage with it during the period on which the allocation of voting power is determined, the articles or bylaws must provide that the member shall nevertheless be allocated a vote equal to at least the minimum voting power allocated to members who used the association or conducted patronage with it during the period.

findings.finding: Investor members each have one vote unless the articles or bylaws otherwise provide; no cap is stated.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: If the articles or bylaws provide for investor members, each investor member has one vote unless the articles or bylaws otherwise provide.

findings.finding: Unless the articles or bylaws otherwise provide, all profits and losses are allocated to patron members.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: Unless the articles or bylaws otherwise provide, all profits and losses of a limited cooperative association must be allocated to patron members.

findings.finding: If an LCA has investor members the articles or bylaws may not reduce the allocation to patron members below fifty percent of profits.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: If a limited cooperative association has investor members, the articles or bylaws may not reduce the allocation to patron members to less than fifty percent of profits.

findings.finding: The board may first set aside unallocated capital and reasonable unallocated reserves, then allocate the remainder to patron members in the ratio of each member's patronage to total patronage.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (5) Subject to subsections (1) and (6) of this section and the articles and bylaws, the board of directors shall allocate the amount remaining after any deduction or setting aside of amounts under subsection (4) of this section: (a) To patron members in the ratio of each member’s patronage to the total patronage of all patron members during the period for which allocations are to be made;

findings.finding: Allocation may be made by pooling arrangements and other equitable methods for patron members (1004(6)).
findings.exactSourceLanguage: for patron members, on class, function, division, district, department, allocation units, pooling arrangements, members’ contributions, or other equitable methods.

findings.finding: Distributions may be in any form, including money, capital credits, allocated patronage equities, revolving fund certificates, and the association's own securities.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: distributions to members may be made in any form, including money, capital credits, allocated patronage equities, revolving fund certificates, and the limited cooperative association’s own or other securities.

findings.finding: No distribution if afterwards the association could not pay debts as they fall due or assets would be less than liabilities (1007(1)).
findings.exactSourceLanguage: A limited cooperative association may not make a distribution if, after the distribution: (a) The association would not be able to pay its debts as they become due in the ordinary course of the association’s activities; or (b) The association’s assets would be less than the sum of its total liabilities.

item.title: Wyoming Decentralized Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act, W.S. 17-32-101 to 17-32-129

findings.finding: A DUNA is an unincorporated nonprofit association with at least one hundred members that elected to form under the Act.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (iii) "Decentralized unincorporated nonprofit association" means an unincorporated nonprofit association that meets the following requirements: (A) Consists of at least one hundred (100) members joined by mutual consent under an agreement, that may be in writing or inferred from conduct, for a common nonprofit purpose;

findings.finding: Governing principles may include smart contracts; membership interest may be ascertained from distributed ledger technology.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: "Membership interest" means a member's voting right in a decentralized unincorporated nonprofit association determined by the decentralized unincorporated nonprofit association's governing principles, including as ascertained from decentralized ledger technology on which the decentralized unincorporated nonprofit association relies to determine a member's voting right;

findings.finding: A DUNA may make profits but must use them for its common nonprofit purpose and may not pay dividends or distribute income or profits to members, administrators or outsiders, except reasonable compensation, benefits conforming to the nonprofit purpose, repurchases, and distributions on winding up.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (b) Except as provided in subsection (c) of this section, a decentralized unincorporated nonprofit association may not pay dividends or distribute any part of its income or profits to its members or administrators or persons outside the decentralized unincorporated nonprofit association. (c) A decentralized unincorporated nonprofit association may: (i) Pay reasonable compensation or reimburse reasonable expenses to its members, administrators and persons outside the decentralized unincorporated nonprofit association for services rendered, including with respect to the administration and operation of the decentralized unincorporated nonprofit association, which may include the provisions of collateral for the self-insurance of the decentralized unincorporated nonprofit association, voting or participation in the decentralized unincorporated nonprofit association's operations and activities; (ii) Confer benefits on its members and administrators in conformity with its common nonprofit purpose; (iii) Repurchase membership interests to the extent authorized by the decentralized unincorporated nonprofit association's governing principles; and (iv) Make distributions of property to members upon winding up and termination of the decentralized unincorporated nonprofit association to the extent permitted by W.S. 17-32-126.

findings.finding: A DUNA is a legal entity separate from its members in contract and tort, and members and administrators are not liable merely by membership.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: is a legal entity separate from its members for the purposes of determining and enforcing rights, duties and liabilities in contract and tort.

item.title: Wyoming Decentralized Autonomous Organization Supplement, W.S. 17-31-101 to 17-31-115

findings.finding: A DAO is a Wyoming LLC whose articles state it is a DAO; the name must include DAO, LAO or DAO LLC; the articles must state how much management is algorithmic.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (a) A decentralized autonomous organization is a limited liability company whose articles of organization contain a statement that the company is a decentralized autonomous organization as described in subsection (c) of this section. (b) A limited liability company formed under the Wyoming Limited Liability Company Act, W.S. 17-29-101 through 17-291102, may convert to a decentralized autonomous organization by amending its articles of organization to include the statement required by subsections (a) and (c) of this section and W.S. 1731-106. (c) A statement in substantially the following form shall appear conspicuously in the articles of organization or operating agreement, if applicable, in a decentralized autonomous organization: NOTICE OF RESTRICTIONS ON DUTIES AND TRANSFERS The rights of members in a decentralized autonomous organization may differ materially from the rights of members in other limited liability companies. The Wyoming Decentralized Autonomous Organization Supplement, underlying smart contracts, articles of organization and operating agreement, if applicable, of a decentralized autonomous organization may define, reduce or eliminate fiduciary duties and may restrict transfer of ownership interests, withdrawal or resignation from the decentralized autonomous organization, return of capital contributions and dissolution of the decentralized autonomous organization. (d) The registered name for a decentralized autonomous organization shall include wording or abbreviation to denote its status as a decentralized autonomous organization, specifically "DAO", "LAO", or "DAO LLC." (e) A statement in the articles of organization shall establish how the decentralized autonomous organization shall be managed by the members, including to what extent the management will be conducted algorithmically.

findings.finding: The articles must include a publicly available identifier of any smart contract directly used to manage, facilitate or operate the DAO.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (b) In addition to the requirements of subsection (a) of this section the articles of organization shall include a publicly available identifier of any smart contract directly used to manage, facilitate or operate the decentralized autonomous organization.

findings.finding: All smart contracts utilized by a DAO LLC must be capable of being updated, modified or otherwise upgraded.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: All smart contracts utilized by a decentralized autonomous organization shall be capable of being updated, modified or otherwise upgraded.

findings.finding: Absent contrary terms, members owe no fiduciary duty beyond the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing; the articles may define, reduce or eliminate fiduciary duties.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: Unless otherwise provided for in the articles of organization or operating agreement, no member of a decentralized autonomous organization shall have any fiduciary duty to the organization or any member except that the members shall be subject to the implied contractual covenant of good faith and fair dealing.

findings.finding: Distributions to members before dissolution are governed by the articles and smart contracts.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (viii) Distributions to members prior to dissolution;

notFound: A rule on patronage-based distributions; the chapter supplies a governance wrapper and no patron/investor classes.

item.title: Wyoming Processing Cooperative Law, W.S. 17-10-201 et seq. (purpose 17-10-205, voting 17-10-230)

findings.finding: A Wyoming cooperative under this article is formed to market, process or change the form or marketability of crops, livestock and other agricultural products and related purposes.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: A cooperative may be formed and organized on a cooperative plan as provided under this article to market, process, or otherwise change the form or marketability of crops, livestock and other agricultural products, including manufacturing and further processing of those products and other purposes that are necessary or convenient to facilitate the production or marketing of agricultural products by patron members and other purposes that are related to the business of the cooperative.

findings.finding: A patron member is entitled to only one vote, and the entire patron voting power is voted collectively by majority of patron members voting.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (a) A patron member of a cooperative is only entitled to one (1) vote on an issue to be voted upon by members holding patron membership interests, except that a patron member of a cooperative described in W.S. 17-10-231 may be entitled to more than one (1) vote as provided in that section. On any matter of the cooperative, the entire patron members voting power shall be voted collectively based upon the vote of the majority of patron members voting on the issue.

notFound: The phrase "limited cooperative" in W.S. Title 17: zero occurrences in the 2026 compilation (801 pages read as text). Wyoming has no uniform limited cooperative association act in Title 17.

item.title: Samuels v. Lido DAO, No. 3:23-cv-06492-VC (N.D. Cal. Nov. 18, 2024), Order denying motions to dismiss, ECF 115

findings.finding: The court held Samuels adequately alleged Lido DAO is a general partnership under California law and not immune from suit, and that Paradigm and Andreessen Horowitz, through governance participation, are plausibly general partners liable for its conduct.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: The first question is whether Lido DAO is capable of being sued. The complaint alleges that it was founded by three investors whose whereabouts are either remote or unknown, and who apparently cannot be hauled into court in the United States. “DAO” stands for Decentralized Autonomous Organization—a type of organization that seems designed, at least in part, to avoid legal liability for its activities. As discussed in Section II of this ruling, Samuels has adequately Case 3:23-cv-06492-VC Document 115 Filed 11/18/24 Page 2 of 28 alleged that Lido DAO is not immune from suit. Specifically, he has alleged that Lido is a general partnership within the meaning of California law.

findings.finding: The court rejected the argument that Lido is merely autonomous software: its actions are the actions of an entity run by people.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: But Lido’s alleged actions are not those of an autonomous software program—they are the actions of an entity run by people.

findings.finding: Governance participation is the partnership fact: investors with the capacity to participate meaningfully in governance plausibly carried on the DAO's business for profit.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: Because the complaint alleges that Paradigm and Andreessen Horowitz participated in Lido DAO governance, it plausibly alleges that they (possibly alongside others) jointly carried on the DAO’s business for profit.

sources.population: tokenholder-governed DAO without a legal wrapper
notFound: This is a ruling on a motion to dismiss accepting the complaint's allegations; no merits judgment.

item.title: CFTC v. Ooki DAO, No. 3:22-cv-05416-WHO (N.D. Cal. June 8, 2023), Order granting default judgment, ECF 76

findings.finding: The court recalls its prior order permitting alternative service and finding Ooki DAO an unincorporated association under California and federal law (line numbers of the pleading paper omitted; the closing words are bracketed).
findings.exactSourceLanguage: finding that Ooki DAO was an unincorporated association as defined by California [and federal law]

notFound: The June 8, 2023 order was read for this recital only; the judgment (ECF 77) was not read for the penalty terms.

item.title: Sarcuni v. bZx DAO, No. 22-cv-618 (S.D. Cal. Mar. 27, 2023), Order on motions to dismiss, ECF 49

findings.finding: The court found the complaint sufficiently alleges the DAO is an association of two or more persons that operates as a business for profit, the elements of a general partnership.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: The Court finds that the FAC sufficiently alleges that the DAO is an association of two or more persons and that it operates as a business for profit.

findings.finding: Plaintiffs' theory: the bZx and Ooki DAOs are general partnerships among tokenholders, each partner jointly and severally liable for the DAO's torts.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: Plaintiffs allege that “[g]iven their structures and the way they operate, the bZx and Ooki DAOs are general partnerships among tokenholders.”

searches.reading: Title 17 of the Wyoming Statutes, 2026 compilation, contains no limited cooperative association act; its cooperative article is the Processing Cooperative Law for agricultural products (17-10-201 et seq.), with patron and nonpatron members (17-10-202) and agricultural purposes (17-10-205). The house draft cites W.S. 17-10-230 as Wyoming's LCA voting default; 17-10-230 is the Processing Cooperative Law's patron-voting section.
